message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for drawing pixels on screen, now also used for massively parallel compute tasks. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32), each highly optimized for complex control flow, low latency, and large caches. | Hundreds or thousands of simpler cores, optimized for throughput and data‑parallel operations. |
| **Instruction set** | Complex instruction set (CISC) with sophisticated branching, caching, and out‑of‑order execution. | Simpler instruction set (SIMD) that can execute the same operation on many data elements simultaneously. |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, deep memory hierarchy, high single‑thread performance. | Smaller per‑core cache; relies on high bandwidth memory (HBM, GDDR) and shared memory pools. |
| **Typical workloads** | Single‑threaded or lightly threaded tasks, heavy branching, I/O, OS services. | Data‑parallel tasks: matrix multiplication, convolution, image processing, machine learning inference/training, scientific simulations. |
| **Performance characteristics** | Low latency, high clock speed, good for tasks that require quick responses. | High throughput, great for tasks that can be split into many independent operations. |
| **Programming model** | Traditional imperative programming, multi‑threading with locks/threads. | SIMD/SIMT programming models (CUDA, OpenCL, Vulkan compute shaders). |
| **Energy efficiency** | Optimized for balanced performance/energy across diverse workloads. | Optimized for raw throughput; can consume more power when fully utilized. |

In short, a CPU excels at handling a wide variety of tasks quickly and efficiently, especially those that involve complex decision making and low latency. A GPU shines when you have a huge amount of data that can be processed in parallel—think rendering millions of pixels or training a neural network on thousands of floating‑point operations. Modern systems often combine both: the CPU manages overall system control while the GPU accelerates specific compute‑heavy or graphics‑heavy parts.
